entity.name: Ibn Khaldun
entity.description: The scholar who invented sociology four centuries early. An Arab historian, philosopher, and political operator who served and betrayed a dozen North African sultans before retreating to an Algerian castle to write the Muqaddimah, a theory of civilizational rise and collapse that anticipated Marx, Adam Smith, and modern economics by hundreds of years.

story.name: Ibn Khaldun
story.description: Plague orphan in Tunis, imprisoned schemer in Fez, diplomat to the King of Castile, fugitive scholar writing in an Algerian fortress, and Grand Judge in Mamluk Cairo. A life of betrayals, exiles, and one world-changing book.

moments.name: Ibn Khaldun Is Born Into an Exiled Andalusian Family in Tunis
moments.subtitle: His ancestors fled Seville 84 years earlier when the Reconquista took the city
moments.description: Tunis in 1332 was the capital of the Hafsid dynasty, its whitewashed medina crowded with mosques, madrasas, and markets serving as a refuge for Andalusian families displaced by the Christian Reconquista. On 27 May 1332, Abd al-Rahman ibn Muhammad ibn Khaldun was born there into one such family — Arab elites who had held high offices in Seville before its fall in 1248. His father and grandfather had withdrawn from politics to join a mystical Sufi order, but the family's scholarly network gave the boy access to the finest teachers in the Maghreb. His brother Yahya would also become a historian — and be assassinated for it.

moments.name: The Black Death Kills Ibn Khaldun's Parents and Teachers in Tunis
moments.subtitle: The 17-year-old loses his entire intellectual world in a single epidemic
moments.description: The plague arrived in Tunis in 1348, carried by ships docking at the city's busy Mediterranean port. Ibn Khaldun, seventeen years old and deep in his studies of the Quran, Arabic linguistics, and Maliki jurisprudence, lost both parents and several of his most important teachers in the same epidemic. The scholars who survived soon departed — Sultan Abu al-Hasan brought them back to Fez, leaving the young Ibn Khaldun stranded. His older brother Muhammad talked him out of following. The catastrophe forced Ibn Khaldun into politics rather than pure scholarship, launching a career of palace intrigues across four countries.

moments.name: Ibn Khaldun Is Imprisoned for 22 Months for Scheming Against the Sultan of Fez
moments.subtitle: The 25-year-old's habit of plotting against employers catches up with him
moments.description: Inside the Marinid royal court at Fez — a city of intricate zellige tilework, towering minarets, and the world's oldest university — Ibn Khaldun had been appointed writer of royal proclamations for Sultan Abu Inan Fares I. But the young scholar could not resist conspiracy. In 1357, his scheming against his own employer was discovered, and the 25-year-old was thrown into prison for 22 months. He was freed only when Abu Inan died in 1358 and the new vizier restored his rank. Ibn Khaldun immediately began plotting against the next sultan, a pattern he would repeat across a dozen North African courts.

moments.name: Ibn Khaldun Negotiates a Peace Treaty with Pedro the Cruel of Castile
moments.subtitle: The Castilian king offers to return his family's lost Spanish estates — he declines
moments.description: In 1364, the Nasrid Sultan Muhammad V of Granada entrusted Ibn Khaldun with a diplomatic mission to Seville to negotiate peace with King Pedro I of Castile, known as Pedro the Cruel. Ibn Khaldun traveled from the red-walled Alhambra palace into Christian Spain, where he met the Castilian monarch in the old Andalusian city his own ancestors had fled a century earlier. Pedro was so impressed that he offered Ibn Khaldun a place at his court and the return of his family's confiscated Spanish properties. Ibn Khaldun politely refused and returned to Granada — where the sultan's vizier, jealous of his influence, soon forced him out.

moments.name: Ibn Khaldun Writes the Muqaddimah in an Algerian Desert Fortress
moments.subtitle: Six months of seclusion produce a theory of civilization that anticipates Marx by 500 years
moments.description: Qalat Ibn Salama was a remote fortress in the hills of western Algeria, sheltered by Berber tribes who owed Ibn Khaldun favors from his years of political dealmaking. Exhausted by decades of switching allegiances across North African courts, the 43-year-old scholar retreated there around 1375 and began writing. In roughly six months, he produced the Muqaddimah — a sweeping introduction to world history that laid out a cyclical theory of how civilizations rise from tribal solidarity, grow wealthy, decay into luxury, and collapse. Modern scholars compare its economic theories to Adam Smith and its sociology to Auguste Comte, both writing centuries later.

moments.name: Ibn Khaldun Dies in Cairo After Serving as Grand Judge Six Times
moments.subtitle: A ship had drowned his wife and children off Alexandria twenty-two years earlier
moments.description: Ibn Khaldun spent his final decades in Mamluk Cairo, the wealthiest city in the Islamic world, where towering minarets and ornate madrasas lined the streets between the Citadel and al-Azhar mosque. Sultan Barquq appointed him Grand Qadi of the Maliki school of law in 1384 — the same year a ship carrying his wife and children sank off Alexandria. Ibn Khaldun tried to reform the Egyptian courts, was forced to resign within a year, then was reappointed to the judgeship five more times. He died on 17 March 1406 in Cairo at age 73. His Muqaddimah was largely forgotten until Ottoman historians rediscovered it two centuries later.
